title: ESSAY 8: Women and Finance — Bridging the Gender Credit Gap

blocks.content: (Word Count: ~310 words | Type: Analytical | Level: NABARD / RBI Grade B / SBI PO)

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The gender credit gap stems from socio-cultural barriers, lack of asset ownership for collateral, and systemic financial exclusion.
PM MUDRA Yojana and Stand-Up India serve as pivotal government frameworks facilitating collateral-free credit to women entrepreneurs.
Self-Help Groups (SHGs) under DAY-NRLM act as the primary catalyst for micro-credit delivery and rural financial empowerment.
Closing the gender credit gap is crucial for enhancing female labor force participation, financial autonomy, and overall GDP growth.

blocks.content: Bridging the gender credit gap is not merely a social obligation, but an economic imperative for sustainable national growth.

Despite constituting nearly half of India's population and contributing substantially to its agricultural and informal economies, women in India face a deeply entrenched gender credit gap — a structural disparity in access to formal financial resources that perpetuates economic inequality and constrains national productivity. A 2023 report by the International Finance Corporation estimates that the formal credit gap for women-owned micro and small enterprises in India exceeds USD 158 billion — a staggering figure that represents not just financial exclusion but wasted economic potential.

rows: At least 1 Woman borrower per bank branch

blocks.content: The barriers are multidimensional. Land and property — the most widely accepted collateral for bank loans — are disproportionately titled in the names of men, leaving women without the asset base necessary for formal credit access. Social norms in many communities restrict women's mobility, limiting their ability to visit bank branches independently or engage with male bank officials. The informal nature of women's income-generating activities — whether through household enterprises, agricultural labour, or handicraft production — makes it difficult to document income flows that formal loan appraisal processes require. Furthermore, low financial literacy among many women borrowers makes them vulnerable to exploitation by informal lenders and, increasingly, by predatory digital lending applications.

India's policy ecosystem has generated significant initiatives to address these barriers. The SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, pioneered by NABARD, has enabled over 10 crore women in more than 90 lakh self-help groups to access collective credit — transforming financial exclusion into economic agency. The Stand-Up India scheme reserves one branch-level loan per bank branch for a woman entrepreneur. The PM Mudra Yojana has disbursed over 68% of its loans to women borrowers. Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana, PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima, and the PM Matru Vandana Yojana have extended financial protection to girl children and mothers.

items: Stand-Up India mandates every bank branch to extend loans between ₹10 lakh and ₹1 crore to at least one SC/ST and at least one woman borrower.
PM MUDRA Yojana offers collateral-free loans across three categories: Shishu (up to ₹50,000), Kishor (₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh), and Tarun (₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh).
NABARD's SHG-Bank Linkage Programme remains the world's largest microfinance project and is frequently tested in banking and civil services exams.

blocks.content: Yet policy intentions must be matched by ground-level execution. Banks must deploy more women Business Correspondents and women relationship managers in rural areas where cultural constraints limit male-female interaction. Loan products must be designed for the asset-light, income-variable profiles of women entrepreneurs. And financial literacy programmes must be conducted in the languages, idioms, and spaces that rural women actually inhabit. Closing the gender credit gap is not a women's issue — it is India's economic imperative.

Examiner's Tip: Essays on women and banking score well when they combine data (USD 158 billion credit gap), government schemes (Stand-Up India, Mudra), and solution-oriented thinking. The phrase 'transforming financial exclusion into economic agency' is memorable and demonstrates eloquence.
